# Presentations

## Starting Today {.plain-title}

::: {.steps}
1. Three groups, drawn at random, at the start of every class
2. Five minutes each, on what you got done last session
3. Show the repository --- the skill, the code, the numbers
:::

::: {.note .note-plum}
What broke is more interesting than what worked, and it is what the rest of the
room needs to hear. A presentation that reports only success is a presentation
nobody learns from.
:::

## What to Cover

::: {.cards .cards-3}
::: {.card}
[What you decided]{.card-title}

Which multiple, which peer group, what minimum size. And why.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[What surprised you]{.card-title}

The company where the answer was obviously wrong, and what it turned out to be.
:::

::: {.card}
[What you would change]{.card-title}

You have run it now. What is the first thing you would do differently?
:::
:::

# From a Gap to a Trade

## You Have a Number for Every Stock

::: {.lead}
Own P/E divided by peer median P/E. Below one is cheap relative to its peers;
above one is expensive.
:::

::: {.note}
That is a prediction, whether or not you meant it as one. It says: this company
should trade closer to its peers than it does.
:::

The question today is whether that prediction is worth anything.

## Sort, Do Not Threshold {.band-bottom}

::: {.cards .cards-2}
::: {.card}
[A threshold]{.card-title}

"Buy anything below 0.7." How many stocks is that? Some years, none. Some years,
four hundred.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[A sort]{.card-title}

"Buy the cheapest tenth." Always the same number of positions, whatever the
market is doing.
:::
:::

::: {.note .note-plum}
Ranking also throws away the scale of the signal, which is the part you trust
least. You are betting on the order, not the magnitude.
:::

## Long, Short, or Both

::: {.cards .cards-3}
::: {.card}
[Long only]{.card-title}

Buy the cheapest decile. Most of what you earn is just the market.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[Long-short]{.card-title}

Cheapest decile long, most expensive short. What is left is the signal.
:::

::: {.card}
[Long-short, dollar neutral]{.card-title}

Equal dollars each side. The version we will build.
:::
:::

::: {.note}
The long-short version is a much harder test, and it is the one that tells you
whether you found anything.
:::

# One Year at a Time

## The Loop {.plain-title}

::: {.steps}
1. Pick a date --- the last trading day of June, say
2. Compute the signal for every stock, using only what was known that day
3. Sort, and form the portfolio
4. Hold it for one year. No trading, no rebalancing
5. Record the return
6. Move forward a year and do it again
:::

::: {.note}
Twenty-odd repetitions. That is your entire sample, and it is worth remembering
how small a number that is.
:::

## Why Once a Year {.compare}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[The signal moves slowly]{.eyebrow}

It is built from annual filings. Recomputing it monthly gives you eleven months
of the same answer and eleven months of trading costs.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
[And it keeps the test honest]{.eyebrow}

Annual holding periods make the overlapping-returns problem go away. Monthly
rebalancing with annual data does not give you twelve times the evidence.
:::
::::

## Equal or Value Weighted {.band-bottom}

::: {.cards .cards-2}
::: {.card}
[Equal weighted]{.card-title}

Same dollars in each name. Simple, and dominated by small companies --- which is
where most anomalies live, and where they are hardest to trade.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[Value weighted]{.card-title}

Weights by market cap. A much more honest test, and usually a much weaker
result.
:::
:::

::: {.note .note-plum}
Report both. A strategy that works equal-weighted and dies value-weighted has
told you exactly what it is.
:::

## Build It

[Tell GLM]{.eyebrow}

> Write a backtest. For each year from 2001 to 2025: on June 30, compute the
> peer-median signal for every stock using the valuation skill, sort into
> deciles, go long the cheapest decile and short the most expensive, equal
> weighted, hold twelve months, and record the return. Plan it before you start.

::: {.note}
Then read the plan before you let it write anything.
:::

# What Would Have Ruined It

## The Restatement Problem

::: {.lead}
`MRY` is the most recent restatement. It tells you today what nobody knew then.
:::

::: {.note .note-plum}
A company that restated its 2008 earnings in 2011 shows up in `MRY` with the
restated number --- so a backtest that forms a 2009 portfolio is using
information from 2011. The strategy will look better than it was.
:::

Use the as-reported dimensions, `ARY` and `ARQ`, for anything historical.

## Filed, Not Ended {.band-bottom}

::: {.cards .cards-2}
::: {.card}
[`reportperiod`]{.card-title}

When the fiscal year ended. Nobody outside the company knew the numbers yet.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[`datekey`]{.card-title}

When it was filed with the SEC. This is the first day you could have acted on it.
:::
:::

::: {.note}
Sorting on `reportperiod` gives you a few weeks to a few months of free
information, every year, in every name. It is the single most common way a
backtest in this course goes wrong.
:::

## Who Is in the Sample

::: {.lead}
Ask a question you cannot answer from the schema: does the data still contain
companies that stopped existing?
:::

::: {.note .note-plum}
If it holds only companies listed today, then every 2005 portfolio you form is
made of firms you already know survived to 2026. That is not a small bias. It is
the difference between a strategy and an illusion.
:::

[Tell GLM]{.eyebrow}

> Count distinct tickers with data in 2005. Then count how many of those still
> have data in the most recent year, and show me some that do not.

## Three More {.plain-title}

| | |
|---|---|
| The peer median | Computed from the same date, or from data that arrived later? |
| Delisting returns | A company that goes to zero has to be recorded as going to zero |
| Costs and borrow | The short side is not free, especially in the small names |

::: {.note}
None of these will throw an error. Each of them makes the answer better than the
truth.
:::

# Reading the Result

## Three Numbers {.band-bottom}

::: {.cards .cards-3}
::: {.card}
[Average return]{.card-title}

The mean of your annual long-short returns.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[Standard deviation]{.card-title}

How much those returns bounced around, year to year.
:::

::: {.card}
[The ratio, and its t-stat]{.card-title}

With twenty-five observations, the t-stat is doing a lot of work.
:::
:::

::: {.note .note-plum}
Twenty-five annual returns is a small sample. A strategy earning four percent a
year with fifteen percent volatility is not distinguishable from nothing.
:::

## Compare It to Something

::: {.lead}
Four percent a year is a fact about your strategy. It is not yet a finding.
:::

::: {.cards .cards-3}
::: {.card}
[The market]{.card-title}

Did the long side simply do what stocks did?
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[A random sort]{.card-title}

Run it with the signal shuffled. What does noise earn in your backtest?
:::

::: {.card}
[Value itself]{.card-title}

Plain P/E, no peer group. Did the peer adjustment add anything?
:::
:::

::: {.note}
The third comparison is the real test of last session's work.
:::

## Look at the Years {.plain-title}

[Tell GLM]{.eyebrow}

> Plot the annual return of the long-short portfolio, year by year. Mark the
> best and worst years and tell me what the portfolio held in each.

::: {.note}
An average built out of one enormous year and twenty-four small negative ones is
a different animal from a steady four percent, and the summary statistics will
not tell you which you have.
:::

# A Memory Your Group Can Read

## Three People, No Shared Memory

::: {.lead}
The conversation you had with GLM on Tuesday is invisible to your groupmates,
and gone to you.
:::

::: {.note .note-plum}
The code survives. The reasoning does not --- why you used `ARY`, which peer
definition you rejected, what you tried on the short side that did not work.
That is exactly what the next person needs, and exactly what nobody writes down.
:::

## What a Memory File Is

::: {.cards .cards-3}
::: {.card}
[One file per session]{.card-title}

Dated, in the repository, next to the code it describes.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[Written by GLM]{.card-title}

At the end of the session, from the conversation it just had. You correct it.
:::

::: {.card}
[Read by GLM]{.card-title}

At the start of the next session, before it touches anything.
:::
:::

::: {.note}
It serves your groupmates and it serves the model. Both start every session
knowing nothing.
:::

## What Goes in It {.band-bottom}

::: {.steps}
1. Date, and who was working
2. What we set out to do
3. What we decided, and what we rejected --- with the reason
4. What broke, and whether it is fixed
5. What is unfinished, and where to pick it up
:::

::: {.note .note-plum}
Point 3 is the one that matters and the one that gets dropped. A decision
without its reason gets re-litigated in two weeks.
:::

## Build the Skill

[Tell GLM]{.eyebrow}

> Make a skill that writes a session memory file. It should trigger when I say
> we are wrapping up. Write to `memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md` with those five headings,
> drawn from this conversation. Keep it under a page.

Then a second one, or a line in `CLAUDE.md`:

> At the start of every session, read the three most recent files in `memory/`.

## Try It Now

::: {.steps}
1. Build the skill
2. Say: we are wrapping up
3. Read what it wrote --- and fix what it got wrong about your own afternoon
4. Commit and push, so the other two can read it before Thursday
:::

::: {.note}
Step 3 is not optional. A memory file nobody checked is a confident record of a
session that did not happen.
:::

# Before Thursday

## Three Things {.plain-title}

::: {.steps}
1. Get the backtest running end to end, however crude
2. Re-run it with `ARY` and `datekey`, and record what changed
3. Write the memory file, and push it
:::

::: {.note .note-plum}
Thursday we stop borrowing the peer median and start predicting the multiple ---
which turns valuation into a regression, and gives you something to compare
today's result against.
:::
